clue.text: Not how this minister would be informally be welcomed in speech!

definitions.text: Not how this minister would be informally be welcomed in speech!

parts.words: Not how this minister would be informally be welcomed in speech!
parts.note: a casual spoken greeting of hello to a cleric sounds just like this senior priest's title, yet nobody would greet so exalted a figure that way

explanation.surface: A remark on the proper etiquette for greeting a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that 'Hi, priest!' is the casual greeting, and the title sounds exactly like it; the clue says that is not how such a figure is greeted. The printed clue has a stray second 'be'.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief cleric of a temple or religion, such as the Jewish chief priest, holds this title.

clue.text: Basil, for example, is one man's name

definitions.meaning: basil is a culinary plant used for flavouring
a short form of the first name Herbert

explanation.surface: A remark that Basil is the name of a certain man.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil looks like a man's name, which is the misdirection: it is the kitchen plant, and the man's name is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is a leafy flavouring plant, and the word is also a familiar shortening of Herbert.

clue.text: Eucalyptus you don't want to climb!

definitions.text: Eucalyptus you don't want to climb!

parts.words: Eucalyptus you don't want to climb!
parts.note: the idiom 'up a' this tree means stuck in serious trouble, so being up one is a place to avoid

explanation.surface: A warning against shinning up a particular Australian tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up a gum tree' is a British and Australian idiom meaning in a hopeless predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: Eucalypts are commonly called by this name in Australia because of their sticky resin.

clue.text: Forecast operating cost needs changing

indicators.note: the letters of the two words before it must be changed around into a new order

explanation.surface: A business note that running costs ought to come down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs changing' rearranges all thirteen letters of OPERATING COST.
explanation.definitionFit: To predict something that has not happened yet is to foretell it, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Violate popular border

parts.note: something in fashion is said to be 'in'
a fringe is an edging or border

explanation.surface: An instruction to cross a well-liked frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: To breach a rule or someone's rights is to transgress against it, a close synonym.

clue.text: Kid hacking into Windows program

indicators.note: the answer breaks into the words that follow, sitting across the join between them

explanation.surface: A youngster breaking into a computer operating system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hacking into' signals letters hidden across windowS PROGram.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a child.

clue.text: Principal cook helping to make lunch effortlessly

indicators.note: helping to make says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A head cook who produces a midday meal with ease.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across lunCH EFfortlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a kitchen is its chief cook; the word comes from French for 'head'.

clue.text: Catch small number giving cheer

parts.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it
ten is a small number

explanation.surface: Grabbing a modest figure that brings encouragement.
explanation.definitionFit: To encourage someone or lift their spirits is to buoy them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Property owner makes no charge on container

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: something free costs nothing
a holder is something that contains

explanation.surface: A landlord who lets a storage vessel free of cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts FREE above HOLDER in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who owns land or a building outright, with no lease, has this kind of tenure.

clue.text: Fellow connected with Italian city and love

parts.note: Rome is the Italian capital
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A man linked with a city in Italy and with romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's lover was from Verona, not Rome, which helps the surface mislead.
explanation.definitionFit: Romeo is a common term for a man, especially an amorous one, and the radio code word for R.

clue.text: One's strong point is catching fish? Just lucky

indicators.note: the strong-point word grips the fish word inside it

parts.note: a forte is something one excels at
tuna is a fish

explanation.surface: An angler's talent for landing fish being put down to luck.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'catching fish' describes the wordplay, not an angler; 'is catching' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone favoured by chance is blessed with good fortune.

clue.text: Regular position of second hand (NB not second-hand)

definitions.text: Regular position of second hand (NB not second-hand)

parts.words: Regular position of second hand (NB not second-hand)
parts.note: a clock's second hand reaches the minute mark at the top once every sixty seconds, while the bracket hints at something brand new rather than used

explanation.surface: A puzzle about where a clock's sweeping hand keeps arriving.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the second hand comes up to the minute regularly; read as a phrase, it means the latest, the opposite of second-hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means modern and current, fully abreast of the latest developments.

clue.text: What operation with needle can give is continuous pain in the side

definitions.text: What operation with needle can give

parts.note: running means unbroken or continuous
a stitch is a sharp pain in the side after exercise

explanation.surface: A surgical procedure that leaves a patient with a lasting ache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operation' suggests surgery; it is sewing, where a needle passes in and out in a simple line.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple sewing technique of evenly spaced in-and-out passes of the needle.

clue.text: Youngster, one on unemployment benefit has little money

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, meaning one
the dole is British slang for state unemployment payments
's is the contraction of has
a cent is a coin of small value

explanation.surface: A young person claiming benefit with barely any cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The dole' is everyday British slang for unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager, someone between childhood and adulthood, is a youngster.

clue.text: Doctor wise to secure two points in equestrian routine

indicators.note: the doctor and wise words hold the two compass points between them

parts.note: sage means wise
E and S, east and south, are two compass points

explanation.surface: A clever vet managing to win points in a horse show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' is the container signal: the doctor and the wise word, side by side, hold the two compass points between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitive horse discipline in which the rider guides the horse through precise set movements.

clue.text: Note no thanks brought back, not in any mode

indicators.note: the three pieces that come before are all read from right to left

parts.note: la is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale
taken as written
ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: Someone returning a musical note and refusing gratitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses LA+NO+TA as one run, giving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Music with no key or tonal centre is written in no major or minor scale.

clue.text: City that's singularly loaded importing gold

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take in the gold letters
used in its sense of strangely or oddly, telling us the letters of loaded are jumbled

parts.note: or is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: A remarkably rich city bringing in bullion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singularly' rearranges LOADED into ELDADO, and 'importing' takes the gold letters into it, so the surface's rich city is also the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary South American city of gold sought by Spanish explorers.

clue.text: A vital developing country

indicators.note: what develops changes shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that a crucial nation is still growing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developing' rearranges the letters of A VITAL.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Baltic state in northern Europe, with Riga its capital.

clue.text: African capital said to give you threefold ecstasy!

indicators.note: the clue words are to be spoken out loud and heard as another word

parts.note: threefold is triple and ecstasy is the drug, E, so three-times E is said as triple E

explanation.surface: A city reputed to offer unbounded rapture.
explanation.walkthrough: E is a slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy; 'triple E' spoken sounds like the city.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital of Libya, on the North African coast.

clue.text: Rueful Chief Executive about to produce tobacco

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a new order

parts.note: CE is the abbreviation for Chief Executive

explanation.surface: A regretful company boss on the verge of making cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges RUEFUL plus CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco leaf is dried with heat from pipes so that it is ready for smoking; the verb names that process.

clue.text: In Paris a free ride is free

parts.note: un is French for a
a hitch is a lift obtained by hitchhiking

explanation.surface: Getting a lift without charge in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' appears twice: in 'free ride' it is part of the lift, and at the end it is the verb meaning release.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfasten a horse or trailer is to release it, so the verb means set loose.

clue.text: Personal cleaning service? Boots could profit from it

definitions.text: Personal cleaning service? Boots could profit from it

parts.words: Personal cleaning service? Boots could profit from it
parts.note: a soldier's method of shining footwear using saliva and wax, which the surface disguises as a chemist chain selling a hygiene service

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a high-street chemist could sell a grooming service.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots is a British chain of chemists' shops, which is the misdirection; the boots here are footwear given a military shine.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a meticulous shine on military footwear, and by extension great smartness and attention to appearance.

clue.text: Boring exercise?

definitions.meaning: making a hole with a rotating tool
repetitive training, as in military parade practice

explanation.surface: A complaint about a tedious workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' seems to mean dull, but it describes the tool that makes holes; the question mark flags the double meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Repetitive military training is called this, as is the rotating tool that bores holes.

clue.text: Mock joker heartlessly

indicators.note: the centre of the joker word is removed, leaving only its outer parts

parts.note: a jester is a joker at court

explanation.surface: A taunt aimed at a cruel clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' removes ST, the middle two letters of JESTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride or taunt someone with scornful shouts is to ridicule them.

clue.text: Obscure things floating to sea around Morecamble, for example

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit around the comedian's name
loose and drifting, so the letters of to sea move about into a new order

parts.note: Eric Morecambe was a much-loved British comedian, so his surname stands for his first name

explanation.surface: Arcane items drifting out to sea near a Lancashire resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe is also a Lancashire seaside town, the misdirection. 'floating' rearranges TO SEA into ESOTA, and 'around' wraps those letters about the comedian's first name. The clue misspells Morecambe.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric matters known only to a small circle of initiates are arcane or recondite.

clue.text: Release from BBC needing no introduction

indicators.note: the opening letter of the broadcaster's nickname is dropped

parts.note: Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC

explanation.surface: Someone leaving the broadcaster who is famous enough to need no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needing no introduction' drops A, the first letter of AUNTIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or loosen bonds is to set free, so the verb means unbind.

clue.text: Neat cut

explanation.surface: A tidy haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means tidy and well kept; as a verb it means to clip, as with a hedge or hair.

clue.text: One learner has to annoy the lady totally

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, meaning one
L is for learner, from British learner-driver plates
get, informally, means irritate
her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: A novice driver set on irritating a woman completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link; GET in the sense 'it really gets me' means annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means completely or in all respects, a synonym of wholly.
